length.text: Females about 81 cm, males about 70 cm on average; up to 135 cm

reproduction.text: Live young, about 8 on average (up to 30)

diet.text: Fish, frogs and tadpoles, plus many other small animals

overview.text: The Common Watersnake (Northern Water Snake) is a large, non-venomous snake of eastern and central North America. It is often mistaken for the venomous Cottonmouth.

identification.text: Brown, grey, reddish or brownish-black with dark crossbands near the head and blotches further back; the pattern can fade as it gets older.

size.label: Adults
size.text: Up to 135 cm. In one study females averaged 81.4 cm and males 69.6 cm; females are heavier too.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: Eastern and central North America, from southern Ontario and Quebec south to the Gulf states, and west to Colorado.

distribution.label: Introduced
distribution.text: An introduced population was found in California in 2007.

behaviour.text: Active by day and by night and often seen basking on rocks, stumps or branches near water.

diet.text: By day it hunts among water plants for small fish, tadpoles, frogs, crayfish, insects, salamanders and more; at night it catches minnows resting in shallow water.

reproduction.text: Mates from April to June and gives birth to live young between August and October - about eight on average, but up to 30. The babies are 19 to 23 cm long and look after themselves from birth.

recognise.text: Dark crossbands and blotches on a brown or grey body.
